narrative:
The model determined that you have a 55% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Three factors drove this outcome, ranked by importance. Your LSAT score had the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. At 26, it sits well below the average of 37 among students who were accepted, signaling weaker preparation in the skills the bar exam tests. Your undergraduate GPA came next and also worked against you. A 2.8 GPA is noticeably lower than the 3.23 average of accepted students, further increasing the estimated risk of failing the bar. 

Family income worked in the opposite direction. Being in the high-income bracket slightly improved the model’s outlook, since most accepted students come from upper-middle or middle brackets and very few from high-income families are in the data. However, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the academic signals.

In short, the decision came down to your LSAT and college grades indicating a higher likelihood of struggling with the bar exam. To strengthen future applications, focus on raising your LSAT score through targeted preparation, as this factor carried the most weight. Improving your study plan now can directly address the main reason for the rejection. (218 words)
